claim: Mutations in the genes for PINK1 and parkin cause Parkinson's disease.
source: Mutations in the genes for PINK1 and parkin cause Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by scientific consensus and literature.

claim: PINK1 and parkin cooperate in the selective autophagic degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) in cultured cells.
source: PINK1 and parkin cooperate in the selective autophagic degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) in cultured cells.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about PINK1/parkin function in cell culture systems.

claim: Evidence for the role of PINK1 and parkin in mitophagy in vivo is scarce.
source: However, evidence for their role in mitophagy in vivo is still scarce.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature, based on inference from available studies.

claim: Mitophagy occurs in muscle cells in vivo in Drosophila, even in the absence of exogenous mitochondrial toxins.
source: Here, we generated a Drosophila model expressing the mitophagy probe mt-Keima. Using live mt-Keima imaging and correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM), we show that mitophagy occurs in muscle cells and dopaminergic neurons in vivo, even in the absence of exogenous mitochondrial toxins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mt-Keima imaging and CLEM presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitophagy occurs in dopaminergic neurons in vivo in Drosophila, even in the absence of exogenous mitochondrial toxins.
source: Here, we generated a Drosophila model expressing the mitophagy probe mt-Keima. Using live mt-Keima imaging and correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM), we show that mitophagy occurs in muscle cells and dopaminergic neurons in vivo, even in the absence of exogenous mitochondrial toxins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mt-Keima imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitophagy increases with aging in Drosophila.
source: Mitophagy increases with aging, and this age-dependent rise is abrogated by PINK1 or parkin deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased mitophagy in older flies as shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The age-dependent rise in mitophagy is abrogated by PINK1 deficiency.
source: Mitophagy increases with aging, and this age-dependent rise is abrogated by PINK1 or parkin deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PINK1B9 mutant flies shown in Figure 3.

claim: The age-dependent rise in mitophagy is abrogated by parkin deficiency.
source: Mitophagy increases with aging, and this age-dependent rise is abrogated by PINK1 or parkin deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from parkin RNAi flies shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Knockdown of the Drosophila homologue of USP15 rescues mitophagy in parkin-deficient flies.
source: Knockdown of the Drosophila homologues of the deubiquitinases USP15 and, to a lesser extent, USP30, rescues mitophagy in the parkin-deficient flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Knockdown of the Drosophila homologue of USP30 rescues mitophagy in parkin-deficient flies to a lesser extent than USP15 knockdown.
source: Knockdown of the Drosophila homologues of the deubiquitinases USP15 and, to a lesser extent, USP30, rescues mitophagy in the parkin-deficient flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in PARK2 and PINK1 are the most prevalent recessive causes of Parkinson's disease.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in PARK2 and PINK1, which encode the cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin and the mitochondrial ubiquitin kinase PINK1, respectively, are the most prevalent recessive causes of Parkinson's disease (PD), an age-dependent neurodegenerative disorder (Corti et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Corti et al., 2011.

claim: Parkinson's disease is an age-dependent neurodegenerative disorder.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in PARK2 and PINK1, which encode the cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin and the mitochondrial ubiquitin kinase PINK1, respectively, are the most prevalent recessive causes of Parkinson's disease (PD), an age-dependent neurodegenerative disorder (Corti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Parkinson's disease.

claim: PARK2 encodes the cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in PARK2 and PINK1, which encode the cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin and the mitochondrial ubiquitin kinase PINK1, respectively, are the most prevalent recessive causes of Parkinson's disease (PD), an age-dependent neurodegenerative disorder (Corti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the PARK2 gene.

claim: PINK1 encodes the mitochondrial ubiquitin kinase PINK1.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in PARK2 and PINK1, which encode the cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin and the mitochondrial ubiquitin kinase PINK1, respectively, are the most prevalent recessive causes of Parkinson's disease (PD), an age-dependent neurodegenerative disorder (Corti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the PINK1 gene.

claim: Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 is stabilized on the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 is stabilized on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and phosphorylates ubiquitin and parkin at their respective S65 residues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PINK1 function, supported by the citation to Pickrell and Youle, 2015.

claim: PINK1 phosphorylates ubiquitin at S65 residue upon mitochondrial damage.
source: Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 is stabilized on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and phosphorylates ubiquitin and parkin at their respective S65 residues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PINK1 function.

claim: PINK1 phosphorylates parkin at S65 residue upon mitochondrial damage.
source: Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 is stabilized on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and phosphorylates ubiquitin and parkin at their respective S65 residues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PINK1 function.

claim: Phosphorylation by PINK1 activates parkin to catalyze ubiquitination of many outer mitochondrial membrane proteins.
source: This activates parkin to catalyze ubiquitination of many OMM proteins that are then either degraded by the proteasome or act as signals for autophagic clearance of the mitochondrion (Pickrell and Youle, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickrell and Youle, 2015.

claim: Ubiquitinated outer mitochondrial membrane proteins are either degraded by the proteasome or act as signals for autophagic clearance of the mitochondrion.
source: This activates parkin to catalyze ubiquitination of many OMM proteins that are then either degraded by the proteasome or act as signals for autophagic clearance of the mitochondrion (Pickrell and Youle, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickrell and Youle, 2015.

claim: Parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination is counteracted by specific deubiquitinases.
source: Parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination and mitophagy are counteracted by specific deubiquitinases (Bingol et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bingol et al., 2014 and Cornelissen et al., 2014.

claim: Parkin-mediated mitophagy is counteracted by specific deubiquitinases.
source: Parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination and mitophagy are counteracted by specific deubiquitinases (Bingol et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bingol et al., 2014 and Cornelissen et al., 2014.

claim: PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy can be triggered in neuronal cells in vitro by exposure to mitochondrial depolarizing agents.
source: PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy can be triggered in a variety of neuronal and non-neuronal cells in vitro, typically by exposure to mitochondrial depolarizing agents (Narendra et al., 2008; Geisler et al., 2010; Cai et al., 2012; Ashrafi et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy can be triggered in non-neuronal cells in vitro by exposure to mitochondrial depolarizing agents.
source: PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy can be triggered in a variety of neuronal and non-neuronal cells in vitro, typically by exposure to mitochondrial depolarizing agents (Narendra et al., 2008; Geisler et al., 2010; Cai et al., 2012; Ashrafi et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy contributes to the maintenance of a healthy mitochondrial network.
source: Along with other mitochondrial quality control mechanisms PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy contributes to the maintenance of a healthy mitochondrial network (Pickles et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickles et al., 2018.

claim: Questions still surround the existence and physiological relevance of PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy in vivo.
source: Despite the wealth of mechanistic information on PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy in cultured cells, questions still surround the existence and physiological relevance of this pathway in vivo (Cummins and Götz, 2018; Whitworth and Pallanck, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cummins and Götz, 2018 and Whitworth and Pallanck, 2017.

claim: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub) is a biomarker of PINK1 activity.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub), a biomarker of PINK1 activity, accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects (Fiesel et al., 2015) and from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading (Pickrell et al., 2015), suggesting that PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging and accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fiesel et al., 2015 and Pickrell et al., 2015.

claim: pS65-Ub accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub), a biomarker of PINK1 activity, accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects (Fiesel et al., 2015) and from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading (Pickrell et al., 2015), suggesting that PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging and accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fiesel et al., 2015.

claim: pS65-Ub accumulates in brains from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub), a biomarker of PINK1 activity, accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects (Fiesel et al., 2015) and from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading (Pickrell et al., 2015), suggesting that PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging and accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickrell et al., 2015.

claim: PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub), a biomarker of PINK1 activity, accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects (Fiesel et al., 2015) and from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading (Pickrell et al., 2015), suggesting that PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging and accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of pS65-Ub in elderly subjects.

claim: PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at S65 (pS65-Ub), a biomarker of PINK1 activity, accumulates in brains from elderly human subjects (Fiesel et al., 2015) and from mice with a genetic defect in mitochondrial DNA proofreading (Pickrell et al., 2015), suggesting that PINK1-mediated mitophagy is induced by aging and accumulation of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of pS65-Ub in mice with mitochondrial DNA defects.

claim: A recent study reported that mitophagy occurs independently of PINK1 in the mouse.
source: However, a recent study reported that mitophagy occurs independently of PINK1 in the mouse (McWilliams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McWilliams et al., 2018.

claim: Deficiency of PINK1 in Drosophila causes reduced life span.
source: In Drosophila, deficiency of PINK1 or parkin causes reduced life span and severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria (Greene et al., 2003; Pesah et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deficiency of parkin in Drosophila causes reduced life span.
source: In Drosophila, deficiency of PINK1 or parkin causes reduced life span and severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria (Greene et al., 2003; Pesah et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deficiency of PINK1 in Drosophila causes severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria.
source: In Drosophila, deficiency of PINK1 or parkin causes reduced life span and severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria (Greene et al., 2003; Pesah et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deficiency of parkin in Drosophila causes severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria.
source: In Drosophila, deficiency of PINK1 or parkin causes reduced life span and severe flight muscle degeneration with accumulation of swollen mitochondria (Greene et al., 2003; Pesah et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In parkin mutant flies, half-lives of mitochondrial proteins are drastically prolonged.
source: In parkin mutant flies, half-lives of mitochondrial proteins are drastically prolonged, consistent with a role for parkin in mitophagy, but the effect of PINK1 on mitochondrial protein turnover is much more limited (Vincow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vincow et al., 2013.

claim: The effect of PINK1 on mitochondrial protein turnover is much more limited than the effect of parkin.
source: In parkin mutant flies, half-lives of mitochondrial proteins are drastically prolonged, consistent with a role for parkin in mitophagy, but the effect of PINK1 on mitochondrial protein turnover is much more limited (Vincow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vincow et al., 2013.

claim: The mt-Keima reporter is a mitochondrially targeted form of Keima.
source: The mt-Keima reporter is a mitochondrially targeted form of Keima, a fluorescent protein that resists degradation by lysosomal proteases (Katayama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Katayama et al., 2011.

claim: Keima is a fluorescent protein that resists degradation by lysosomal proteases.
source: The mt-Keima reporter is a mitochondrially targeted form of Keima, a fluorescent protein that resists degradation by lysosomal proteases (Katayama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Katayama et al., 2011.

claim: The peak of the mt-Keima excitation spectrum shifts when mitochondria are delivered to acidic lysosomes.
source: The peak of the mt-Keima excitation spectrum shifts when mitochondria are delivered to acidic lysosomes, which allows dual-excitation ratiometric quantification of mitophagy (Katayama et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Katayama et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: mt-Keima expression did not change the morphology of muscle mitochondria.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis showed that mt-Keima expression did not change the morphology of muscle mitochondria (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mt-Keima signal extensively colocalized with the mitochondrial protein ATP synthase β.
source: The mt-Keima signal extensively colocalized with the mitochondrial protein ATP synthase β, confirming that mt-Keima was properly targeted to mitochondria (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A small subset of mt-Keima structures had high 543 nm/458 nm ratio values, indicative of an acidic environment.
source: Interestingly, a small subset of mt-Keima structures had high 543 nm/458 nm ratio values, indicative of an acidic environment (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: High 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta colocalized with the lysosomal dye LysoTracker.
source: These high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta colocalized with the lysosomal dye LysoTracker (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta probably represented mitochondria that had been delivered to lysosomes.
source: Thus, the high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta probably represented mitochondria that had been delivered to lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization with LysoTracker and the acidic pH indicated by the ratio.

claim: The abundance of high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta was very low in muscle cells of 1-week-old adult flies.
source: The abundance of these puncta was very low in muscle cells of 1-week-old adult flies, but strongly rose with aging, showing an approximately tenfold increase by the age of 4 weeks (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The abundance of high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta strongly rose with aging, showing an approximately tenfold increase by the age of 4 weeks.
source: The abundance of these puncta was very low in muscle cells of 1-week-old adult flies, but strongly rose with aging, showing an approximately tenfold increase by the age of 4 weeks (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Atg1/ULK1 is needed in the early steps of autophagosome formation.
source: Atg1/ULK1 is needed in the early steps of autophagosome formation and is also involved in mitophagy (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010; Itakura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Itakura and Mizushima, 2010 and Itakura et al., 2012.

claim: Atg1/ULK1 is involved in mitophagy.
source: Atg1/ULK1 is needed in the early steps of autophagosome formation and is also involved in mitophagy (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010; Itakura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Itakura and Mizushima, 2010 and Itakura et al., 2012.

claim: When overexpressed, kinase-dead Atg1 exerts dominant-negative effects.
source: When overexpressed, kinase-dead Atg1 exerts dominant-negative effects (Scott et al., 2007).

claim: Overexpression of Atg1K38A suppressed the high levels of mitophagy observed in aged muscle cells.
source: Overexpression of Atg1K38A suppressed the high levels of mitophagy observed in aged muscle cells (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The low residual level of high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta that persisted after Atg1K38A overexpression may result from Atg1-independent mechanisms of autophagy induction.
source: The low residual level of high 543/458 ratio mt-Keima puncta that persisted after Atg1K38A overexpression, may result from Atg1-independent mechanisms of autophagy induction (Braden and Neufeld, 2016).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Braden and Neufeld, 2016.

claim: 'Neutral pH' mt-Keima structures colocalized with typical mitochondria at the TEM level.
source: Interestingly, 'neutral pH' mt-Keima structures colocalized with typical mitochondria at the TEM level, while 'acidic' mt-Keima puncta showed remarkable overlay with smaller organelles with the characteristic electron-dense appearance of lysosomes (Figure 2E–N).
evidence: This is supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 2E-N.

claim: 'Acidic' mt-Keima puncta showed remarkable overlay with smaller organelles with the characteristic electron-dense appearance of lysosomes.
source: Interestingly, 'neutral pH' mt-Keima structures colocalized with typical mitochondria at the TEM level, while 'acidic' mt-Keima puncta showed remarkable overlay with smaller organelles with the characteristic electron-dense appearance of lysosomes (Figure 2E–N).
evidence: This is supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 2E-N.

claim: Many of the mt-Keima-positive lysosomes contained densely packed concentric membranes surrounding a dense core, giving them the appearance of multilamellar bodies.
source: Many of the mt-Keima-positive lysosomes contained densely packed concentric membranes surrounding a dense core, giving them the appearance of multilamellar bodies (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Multilamellar bodies are lysosomal organelles that are found in various cell types in physiological conditions.
source: Multilamellar bodies are lysosomal organelles that are found in various cell types in physiological conditions but also accumulate in lysosomal storage diseases (Blanchette-Mackie, 2000; Hariri et al., 2000; Lajoie et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blanchette-Mackie, 2000; Hariri et al., 2000; Lajoie et al., 2005.

claim: Multilamellar bodies accumulate in lysosomal storage diseases.
source: Multilamellar bodies are lysosomal organelles that are found in various cell types in physiological conditions but also accumulate in lysosomal storage diseases (Blanchette-Mackie, 2000; Hariri et al., 2000; Lajoie et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blanchette-Mackie, 2000; Hariri et al., 2000; Lajoie et al., 2005.

claim: The low level of mitophagy in 1-week-old adult flies was not affected by deficiency of PINK1.
source: The low level of mitophagy in 1-week-old adult flies was not affected by deficiency of PINK1 or parkin (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The low level of mitophagy in 1-week-old adult flies was not affected by deficiency of parkin.
source: The low level of mitophagy in 1-week-old adult flies was not affected by deficiency of PINK1 or parkin (Figure 3A,B).

claim: The age-dependent increase in mitophagy in 3- and 4-week-old control flies was completely abolished in the parkin RNAi flies.
source: However, the age-dependent increase in mitophagy in 3- and 4-week-old control flies was completely abolished in the PINK1B9 and parkin RNAi flies (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The DUBs USP15 and USP30 oppose parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination in cultured human cells.
source: The DUBs USP15 and USP30 oppose parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination and mitophagy in cultured human cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies in the field.

claim: The DUBs USP15 and USP30 oppose parkin-mediated mitophagy in cultured human cells.
source: The DUBs USP15 and USP30 oppose parkin-mediated mitochondrial ubiquitination and mitophagy in cultured human cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies in the field.

claim: The yeast homologue of USP15 (Ubp12) deubiquitinates the MOM protein Fzo1.
source: Interestingly, the yeast homologue of USP15 (Ubp12) deubiquitinates the MOM protein Fzo1, the yeast homologue of the mammalian parkin substrates mitofusin 1 and 2, pointing to a conserved role for USP15 in deubiquitination at the MOM (Anton et al., 2013; SimoesSimões et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anton et al., 2013 and Simões et al., 2018.

claim: Fzo1 is the yeast homologue of the mammalian parkin substrates mitofusin 1 and 2.
source: Interestingly, the yeast homologue of USP15 (Ubp12) deubiquitinates the MOM protein Fzo1, the yeast homologue of the mammalian parkin substrates mitofusin 1 and 2, pointing to a conserved role for USP15 in deubiquitination at the MOM (Anton et al., 2013; SimoesSimões et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein homology.

claim: There is a conserved role for USP15 in deubiquitination at the mitochondrial outer membrane.

claim: Knockdown of dUSP15 and dUSP30 largely rescues the mitochondrial defects of parkin-deficient fly muscle in vivo.
source: Knockdown of the Drosophila homologs of USP15 (CG8334, hereafter called dUSP15) and USP30 (CG3016, hereafter dUSP30) largely rescues the mitochondrial defects of parkin-deficient fly muscle in vivo (Bingol et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014).

claim: Levels of dUSP15 mRNA in dUSP15 RNAi lines were 57.6 ± 2.5% of control levels.
source: Levels of dUSP15 mRNA in dUSP15 RNAi lines were 57.6 ± 2.5% of control levels (n = 6), and dUSP30 mRNA levels in dUSP30 RNAi lines were 16.4 ± 5.8% of controls (n = 6).

claim: dUSP30 mRNA levels in dUSP30 RNAi lines were 16.4 ± 5.8% of controls.
source: Levels of dUSP15 mRNA in dUSP15 RNAi lines were 57.6 ± 2.5% of control levels (n = 6), and dUSP30 mRNA levels in dUSP30 RNAi lines were 16.4 ± 5.8% of controls (n = 6).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from the study.

claim: Knockdown of dUSP15 rescued the mitophagy defect of two different parkin RNAi fly lines.
source: Knockdown of dUSP15 and, to a lesser extent, dUSP30 rescued the mitophagy defect of two different parkin RNAi fly lines (Figure 3C,D).

claim: Knockdown of dUSP30 rescued the mitophagy defect of two different parkin RNAi fly lines to a lesser extent than dUSP15 knockdown.
source: Knockdown of dUSP15 and, to a lesser extent, dUSP30 rescued the mitophagy defect of two different parkin RNAi fly lines (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The mitophagy defect of PINK1B9 flies was partially rescued by dUSP15 knockdown.
source: The mitophagy defect of PINK1B9 flies was partially rescued by dUSP15 knockdown, but unaffected by dUSP30 knockdown (Figure 3C,D).

claim: The mitophagy defect of PINK1B9 flies was unaffected by dUSP30 knockdown.
source: The mitophagy defect of PINK1B9 flies was partially rescued by dUSP15 knockdown, but unaffected by dUSP30 knockdown (Figure 3C,D).

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of parkin mutant Drosophila accumulate abnormal mitochondria.
source: Dopaminergic neurons of parkin mutant Drosophila also accumulate abnormal mitochondria (Burman et al., 2012).

claim: Mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons increased with aging.

claim: Loss of parkin suppressed mitophagy in 4-week-old dopaminergic neurons.
source: Loss of parkin suppressed mitophagy in 4-week-old flies (Figure 4A,B), and this deficit was rescued by dUSP15 knockdown (Figure 4C,D).

claim: The mitophagy deficit caused by loss of parkin in dopaminergic neurons was rescued by dUSP15 knockdown.
source: Loss of parkin suppressed mitophagy in 4-week-old flies (Figure 4A,B), and this deficit was rescued by dUSP15 knockdown (Figure 4C,D).

claim: PINK1 and parkin appear to be particularly important for mitophagy during aging.
source: Thus, PINK1 and parkin appear to be particularly important for mitophagy during aging, which may explain why loss of these proteins in patients causes an age-dependent neurodegenerative disease rather than a congenital or developmental disorder.

claim: Loss of PINK1 and parkin in patients causes an age-dependent neurodegenerative disease rather than a congenital or developmental disorder because these proteins are particularly important for mitophagy during aging.

claim: pS65-Ub is almost undetectable in postmortem brains from neurologically normal, young human subjects.
source: Consistent with this, pS65-Ub, a readout of PINK1 activity, is almost undetectable in postmortem brains from neurologically normal, young human subjects, but accumulates in brains from elderly individuals (Fiesel et al., 2015).

claim: pS65-Ub accumulates in brains from elderly individuals.

claim: The mito-QC reporter is targeted to the outer mitochondrial membrane.

evidence: This is established knowledge about the mito-QC reporter.

claim: mt-Keima is localized to the mitochondrial matrix.
source: This conclusion was based on imaging using the mito-QC reporter, which differs from the mt-Keima probe used in our study. mito-QC is targeted to the OMM, whereas mt-Keima is localized to the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mt-Keima probe.

claim: Upon mitochondrial damage, activated parkin ubiquitinates a wide variety of outer mitochondrial membrane proteins.
source: Upon mitochondrial damage, activated parkin ubiquitinates a wide variety of OMM proteins, many of which are then extracted from the OMM and degraded by the proteasome before engulfment of the mitochondrion into an autophagosome (Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Sarraf et al., 2013.

claim: Many ubiquitinated outer mitochondrial membrane proteins are extracted from the OMM and degraded by the proteasome before engulfment of the mitochondrion into an autophagosome.
source: Upon mitochondrial damage, activated parkin ubiquitinates a wide variety of OMM proteins, many of which are then extracted from the OMM and degraded by the proteasome before engulfment of the mitochondrion into an autophagosome (Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Sarraf et al., 2013.

claim: The mito-QC probe consists of a tandem mCherry-GFP tag fused to a large portion of the OMM protein FIS1.
source: The mito-QC probe consists of a tandem mCherry-GFP tag fused to a large portion of the OMM protein FIS1 (McWilliams et al., 2016), which is itself a substrate of parkin (Chan et al., 2011; Sarraf et al., 2013).
